t.E296.agn: JECFA has estimated the daily intake of malic acid from vegetables, fruit and fruit juices at 1.5–3 g. In 1991 the EU Scientific Committee on Food (SCF) set the group ADI for malic acid and malates as 'not specified'; JECFA also gave an ADI 'not specified', but stated that for D(-)-malic acid and its salts this value does not apply to very young infants.
t.E296.body: L(+)-malic acid is an intermediate of the Krebs cycle in the body and is readily oxidised; less is known about the fate of the D(-) form in the body.
t.E296.eff.1.t: For D(-)-malic acid and its salts, the daily limit does not apply to very young infants
t.E296.found.0: May be used in many foods in the EU at quantum satis (as much as needed)
t.E296.prod: DL-malic acid is produced by chemical synthesis from petrochemical raw material; its salts are obtained by neutralisation.
t.E296.pw.0: JECFA has recommended that D(-)- and DL-malic acid not be added to foods for very young infants except for therapeutic purposes.
t.E296.regx.0: ADI 'not specified'; for D(-)-malic acid it does not apply to very young infants.
t.E296.regx.1: Group I additive; generally authorised at quantum satis (as much as needed).
t.E296.regx.2: Re-evaluation ongoing; a call for data was published in 2024 (SCF 1991: group ADI 'not specified').
t.E296.summary: An acid found naturally in fruit such as apples. It gives a sour taste and is used in confectionery, beverages and jams.
t.E296.what: It is an acidity regulator that gives food a fruity sourness and adjusts pH.
